# Worksheet: Graphing Effectively

[📥 Download the data (.csv)](data/pine_data.csv){.btn .btn-primary download="pine_data.csv"} [📥 Download the data (.xlsx)](data/pine_data.xlsx){.btn .btn-primary download="pine_data.xlsx"}

> ## How to use this worksheet
>
> Work through each part in order, at your own pace. Type every line of code yourself into a **plain R script** — do not copy-paste. Blocks marked **▶ Run this** are code you should type and execute. Blocks marked **✏️ Your turn** ask you to write, modify, or answer something. Boxes marked **🚀 If you finish early** are optional bonus material.
>
> **Every grey `r` box below is code you type into an R script — not into the Console.** Before you start: **File → New File → R Script**, and save it as `04_graphing_effectively.R` in your project's `scripts/` folder. Then work down the worksheet, adding each block to the bottom of that one script, in order.
>
> **Type the `# ── Part …` header comment at the top of each block, too.** Those comment lines are not decoration — they are how your script stays navigable, how you find your way back to a block that broke, and how I find your work when I read your script. A block with no header comment is a block I cannot place. In RStudio they also show up in the document outline (the `≡` button at the bottom-left of the editor) so you can jump straight to any part.

::: callout-important
## Column names in `pine_data.csv` / `pine_data.xlsx`

Both files hold the **same six columns, with exactly these names**. Type them
exactly as written — R is case-sensitive, and `Needle_Length` or `needle_length`
will not work:

| Column             | What it is                                     |
|--------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| `source_file`      | the raw team file the row came from             |
| `team`             | field team — one team = **one tree**            |
| `replicate`        | needle number within a tree side (1-8)          |
| `side`             | sun exposure — `"shady"` or `"sunny"`           |
| `needle_length_mm` | needle length, millimetres                      |
| `needle_width_mm`  | needle width, millimetres                       |

After you read the file in, run `names(pine_df)` and check the names on your
screen against this table before you write any other code.
:::

# Part 1 · Load the data

**▶ Run this in your Script:**

``` r
# ── Part 1.1 · Load the data ────────────────────────────────────────────
library(tidyverse)

pine_df <- read_csv("data/pine_data.csv")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 2 · Boxplot, from scratch

> 📖 **Read more:** Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 2 (Displaying Data) on Canvas, and [R4DS §9 — Layers](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/layers.html).

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 2.1 · Boxplot, from scratch ────────────────────────────────────
pine_box_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Needle Length by Side of Tree",
    x = "Side of tree", y = "Needle length (mm)", fill = "Side"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

pine_box_plot
```


# Part 3 · Add the raw points

> 📖 **Read more:** Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 2, "How to draw a good graph" — show the data, not only the summary. Also [R4DS §9.6 — Position adjustments](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/layers.html#position-adjustments) for `position_jitter()`.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 3.1 · Add the raw points ───────────────────────────────────────
pine_jitter_plot <- pine_box_plot +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.15),
    alpha = 0.6,
    size = 2
  )

pine_jitter_plot
```

# Part 3b · Axis labels and titles with `labs()`

> 📖 **Read more:** [R4DS §11.1 — Labels](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/communication.html#labels).

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 3b.1 · Axis labels and titles with `labs()` ────────────────────
pine_labeled_plot <- pine_box_plot +
  labs(
    title    = "Needle Length by Side of Tree",
    subtitle = "Four field teams, four trees",
    x        = "Side of tree",
    y        = "Needle length (mm)",
    fill     = "Side",
    caption  = "Data: pine_data.csv"
  )

pine_labeled_plot
```

# Part 4 · Map a third variable with color

> 📖 **Read more:** [R4DS §9.1 — Aesthetic mappings](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/layers.html#aesthetic-mappings).

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 4.1 · Map a third variable with color ──────────────────────────
pine_team_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, color = team)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.15),
    size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(x = "Side of tree", y = "Needle length (mm)", color = "Field team") +
  theme_minimal()

pine_team_plot
```

# Part 4b · Histograms and density curves

> 📖 **Read more:** Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 2 on frequency distributions and bin width; [R4DS §10.3 — Variation](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/EDA.html#variation).

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 4b.1 · Histograms and density curves ───────────────────────────
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = needle_length_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "darkblue", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Needle Length", x = "Needle length (mm)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Try `binwidth = 0.5` and `binwidth = 5`. Which value tells the real story about this data, and which one hides or exaggerates it?

``` r
# ── Part 4b.2 · Histograms and density curves ───────────────────────────
# Write your code here:




```

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 4b.3 · Histograms and density curves ───────────────────────────
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Needle length (mm)", y = "Density", fill = "Side") +
  theme_minimal()
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Do the shady and sunny density curves look like they overlap a lot, or are they clearly separated?

# Part 5 · Mean ± SE, plotted directly

> 📖 **Read more:** Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 4 (Estimating with Uncertainty) — what an error bar actually claims; Gotelli & Ellison Ch. 6 on why independence decides which rows you may average.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 5.1 · Mean ± SE, plotted directly ──────────────────────────────
pine_mean_se_plot <- ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, color = side)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.15),
    alpha = 0.3, size = 2
  ) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 4) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "errorbar", width = 0.15) +
  labs(x = "Side of tree", y = "Needle length (mm)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

pine_mean_se_plot
```

# Part 6 · Facet by field team

> 📖 **Read more:** [R4DS §9.5 — Facets](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/layers.html#facets).

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 6.1 · Facet by field team ──────────────────────────────────────
pine_facet_plot <- pine_box_plot +
  facet_wrap(~team)

pine_facet_plot
```

# Part 8 · Save your figure

> 📖 **Read more:** [R4DS §11 — Communication](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/communication.html), and Whitlock & Schluter Ch. 2 on what a figure must carry to stand on its own.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 8.1 · Save your figure ─────────────────────────────────────────
ggsave(
  "figures/pine_needle_facet_boxplot.png",
  plot   = pine_facet_plot,
  width  = 3,
  height = 3,
  units  = "in",
  dpi    = 300
)
```

Check your `figures/` folder — the PNG should be there.

# Part 8b · Advanced / extra work — `scale_color_manual()`

> 📖 **Read more:** [R4DS §11.4 — Scales](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/communication.html#scales), including the ColorBrewer palettes.

::: callout-tip
**🚀 This part is optional bonus material.** Everything through Part 8 covers the required skills for this module.
:::

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 8b.1 · Advanced / extra work ───────────────────────────────────
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, color = side)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.15), size = 2.5) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 4, color = "black") +
  scale_color_manual(
    name   = "Side of tree",
    labels = c(shady = "Shady side", sunny = "Sunny side"),
    values = c(shady = "#2c7fb8", sunny = "#d95f0e")
  ) +
  labs(x = "Side of tree", y = "Needle length (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

``` r
# ── Part 8b.3 · Advanced / extra work ───────────────────────────────────
ggplot(pine_df, aes(x = side, y = needle_length_mm, fill = side)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(
```

# Readings

**Before next class** — chapter PDFs are posted on **Canvas**:

- **Whitlock & Schluter**, *The Analysis of Biological Data* — **Ch. 2**, Displaying Data. Read "How to draw a good graph" closely: it is the standard every figure you hand in this term is held to
- **Gotelli & Ellison**, *A Primer of Ecological Statistics* — **Ch. 3**, Summary Statistics, for the distributions behind the boxplots and histograms

**If you want more:**

W&S tells you *which* graph is honest; R4DS tells you *how* to draw it. You need both.

# Getting unstuck

When code breaks — and it will, that is normal:

1.  **Read the error message out loud.** R usually names the line and the problem.
2.  **Check the usual suspects:** did you run `library(tidyverse)`? Is `color`/`fill` inside `aes()` when it should be?
3.  `?function_name` opens the built-in help page.
4.  **Bring the exact error** (copy-paste it) to class or office hours.

> 📖 **Read more:** [R4DS §8 — Workflow: getting help](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/workflow-help.html).

> 💡 **Key idea:** Every working scientist googles error messages daily. Getting stuck is not failing — it is the job.
